_readme: What CURRENT (2020s) NASA/ISS astronaut health monitoring actually tracks, for comparison and to drive the app's clearly-labeled 'Modern Monitoring (Simulated)' panel. None of this was measured on Apollo 15 — it did not exist in 1971. Every value the app computes from this file is tagged 'simulated' in the UI, never presented as historical fact.

bio_monitor.name: Bio-Monitor
bio_monitor.developer: Canadian Space Agency (CSA), built by Carré Technologies from their commercial Hexoskin garment
bio_monitor.status: Actively flown on the ISS today — tested by CSA astronaut David Saint-Jacques in 2019 and still in use as of 2025 per NASA's own reporting.
bio_monitor.form_factor: Smart shirt + headband + tablet app; worn under normal clothing, no separate time set aside for readings

parameters.name: Systolic blood pressure
parameters.sensor: Continuous estimate (not a cuff reading) derived from pulse-transit-time

parameters.name: Sleep quality / staging
parameters.sensor: Derived from the above during rest periods

bio_monitor.source: Canadian Space Agency, "Bio-Monitor: Keeping an eye on astronauts' vital signs"; FrogHeart / Waterloo Vascular Aging study (sensor list); NASA ISS blog, Jan 2019; The Industrial Review, "NASA's Health Monitoring Strategy Aboard the ISS," 2025

co2_operational_bands_mmhg.note: Real, current ISS operational guidance — tighter than the NASA-STD-3001 3.0 mmHg design limit, based on directly observed crew symptom reports in recent expeditions.

bands.effect: Self-reported missed procedure steps / procedures running long

co2_operational_bands_mmhg.historical_iss_range: 1-9 mmHg over ISS program history; typical operations now targeted below 3.0 mmHg 24-hour average
co2_operational_bands_mmhg.source: NASA OCHMO-TB-004, "Carbon Dioxide" (Rev C/D, 2022-2023); NASA, "CO2 on the International Space Station: An Operations Update" (NTRS 20150019624)

radiation_modern.note: Apollo 15's dosimeters were passive — read out after splashdown, not monitored in real time. The ISS instead uses continuously-read area and personal dosimetry today.
examples: RaDI-N / RaDI-N2 (Canadian Space Agency): neutron 'bubble detectors' placed around the ISS
Personal and area dosimeters read on an ongoing basis rather than only postflight
radiation_modern.source: NASA ISS On-Orbit Status Report, June 2016 (RaDI-N deployment)

sans.name: Spaceflight Associated Neuro-ocular Syndrome (SANS)
sans.note: A real, actively-studied risk that is specifically DURATION-dependent — about 1 in 3 astronauts on long-duration (months-long) ISS missions show at least one confirmed ocular finding (optic disc edema, globe flattening, choroidal folds, hyperopic shift). Apollo 15 was 12.3 days — far too short for SANS to plausibly develop, which is why it is not modeled as an ongoing risk for this mission, only noted here as a modern contrast.
sans.monitored_today_with: Onboard fundoscopy, optical coherence tomography (OCT), and orbital ultrasound
sans.source: Wikipedia, "Spaceflight associated neuro-ocular syndrome"; Brunstetter T., NASA JSC, "Introduction to SANS" (NTRS 20170009173); Frontiers in Neurology, 2021

behavioral_health.name: Behavioral Health and Performance (BHP) monitoring
behavioral_health.note: Modern crews are tracked for fatigue, workload, and psychological wellbeing through private weekly conferences with a flight surgeon and dedicated software, not a single daily 1-5 self-report — the simplified slider in this app's Wellbeing Check-In is a teaching simplification of this, not a real instrument.
behavioral_health.example_tool: Behavioral Health and Performance Dashboard (BHP-DS), built on the Circadian Performance Simulation Software (Harvard Biomathematical Modeling Unit)
